prompt: Which services can be reached through a gateway endpoint?
hint: Two, and the transcript printed both with `Gateway` beside them.

choices.text: S3 and STS
choices.why: STS appeared only as `Interface`. Of the two, only S3 has a gateway endpoint.

choices.text: S3 and DynamoDB
choices.why: Right. Every other service is reached through an interface endpoint, and S3 has both kinds.

choices.text: DynamoDB and CloudWatch Logs
choices.why: CloudWatch Logs is reached through an interface endpoint, by the hour and the gigabyte.

choices.text: Every service that also has an interface endpoint
choices.why: Hundreds of services have an interface endpoint; two have a gateway one.

prompt: After the gateway endpoint exists, `private-a` sends a packet for S3 to `vpce-…` and not to `nat-a`, although `0.0.0.0/0` matches it too. Why?
hint: Lesson 17's rule for two matching routes.

choices.text: The endpoint's route was added last, and the newest route wins
choices.why: The order routes were written in plays no part; the prefix length does.

choices.text: One of the prefix list's ranges is longer than `0.0.0.0/0`
choices.why: Right. A packet for S3 falls inside one of the list's ranges, and any range is more specific than `/0`.

choices.text: Gateway endpoints always take priority over NAT gateways
choices.why: There is no priority by kind of target. The same longest-prefix rule decides every route.

choices.text: The NAT gateway refuses traffic for AWS services
choices.why: It would carry it gladly, at 0.093 a gigabyte, which is what the shop paid before the endpoint.

prompt: Before the endpoint, the shop's 1 TB (1,024 GB) of monthly backups to S3 went through NAT. How many dollars a month of NAT processing was that?
hint: The price per gigabyte from lesson 17.

prompt: What does the policy in `endpoint-s3.json` do?
hint: A resource policy on a door.

choices.text: It grants every principal in the VPC access to the three buckets
choices.why: An endpoint policy grants nothing; a caller still needs an IAM permission of its own.

choices.text: It limits what passes; the caller still needs IAM permission
choices.why: Right. It narrows the free route to the shop's three buckets, so it cannot be used to copy data elsewhere.

choices.text: It replaces the bucket policies of the three buckets
choices.why: The two are separate documents on separate resources, and both apply.

choices.text: It applies to the subnets' traffic to the internet as well, through NAT
choices.why: It applies to what passes through the endpoint and nothing else. Traffic through NAT never meets it.

prompt: On AWS, with the `aws:SourceVpce` policy on `shop-backups`, an administrator with full IAM permissions runs `aws s3 ls s3://shop-backups` from a laptop. What happens?
hint: An explicit deny, and a condition the laptop cannot meet.

choices.text: Allowed, since an administrator's IAM policy outranks a bucket policy
choices.why: An explicit deny wins over any allow, wherever the allow comes from (lesson 8).

choices.text: Refused: the request did not come through the endpoint
choices.why: Right. `aws:SourceVpce` is unset for a request from outside the VPC, so the Deny applies, to administrators too.

choices.text: Allowed, because listing is not an object request
choices.why: That is what moto did, and it is moto's gap. The policy names `s3:*` on the bucket itself, and AWS refuses the listing.

choices.text: Refused, unless the laptop is in `sa-east-1`
choices.why: A region is not a network path. The condition asks which endpoint the request came through.

prompt: In the lab, `put-object` and `get-object` on `shop-backups` were refused with a 403 and the listing went through. What does that transcript establish?
hint: Compare it with what the section says AWS does.

choices.text: moto judged the object requests only, so it shows part of AWS's behaviour
choices.why: Right. AWS would refuse the listing as well, and would let requests through the endpoint pass, which moto cannot show.

choices.text: moto judged every request exactly as AWS would
choices.why: The listing went through in moto and would be refused on AWS.

choices.text: moto ignored the policy, as it ignores every bucket policy
choices.why: It did not ignore it: the two object requests were refused because of it.

choices.text: moto refused them because they came through the endpoint
choices.why: Nothing comes through an endpoint in moto, and the policy refuses what does not.

prompt: What is an interface endpoint, in the VPC?
hint: It has an address and a security group.

choices.text: A line in a route table naming a prefix list
choices.why: That is a gateway endpoint. An interface endpoint is a place, not a route.

choices.text: A network interface, with a private address, per chosen subnet
choices.why: Right. Three subnets named, three interfaces, one per zone.

choices.text: A NAT gateway reserved for one AWS service
choices.why: It translates nothing; the service answers on the interface's private address.

choices.text: A public address that AWS gives the service inside your own VPC
choices.why: The address is private, from the subnet's own range, which is why nothing has to go out.

prompt: The STS endpoint has private DNS turned on. What has to change in the application for it to use the endpoint?
hint: Which name does every SDK call?

choices.text: It must call the endpoint's own DNS name, `vpce-…`
choices.why: That name works, and with private DNS nobody needs it.

choices.text: It must be given the endpoint's private addresses
choices.why: The VPC's resolver hands them out when the usual name is asked for.

choices.text: Nothing: the usual name resolves to the endpoint inside the VPC
choices.why: Right. `sts.sa-east-1.amazonaws.com` gets a different answer inside the VPC, and the code does not move.

choices.text: It needs a newer SDK that knows about endpoints
choices.why: The SDK never learns there is an endpoint; DNS does the work.

prompt: Which VPC attributes must be on for an interface endpoint's private DNS to work? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them, and a new VPC has only one on.

choices.text: `enableDnsSupport`
choices.why: Right. On in a new VPC.

choices.text: `MapPublicIpOnLaunch`
choices.why: That is a subnet's setting about public addresses, and unrelated.

choices.text: `enableDnsHostnames`
choices.why: Right. Off in a new VPC, which is why the lesson switched it on.

choices.text: `AssignIpv6AddressOnCreation`
choices.why: A subnet's IPv6 setting; private DNS works over IPv4.

prompt: An interface endpoint sits in two zones only. With the lesson's prices and 730 hours, how many dollars a month do its hours cost, before any gigabyte?
hint: 0.021 an hour for each zone.

prompt: The NAT gateways stay, for the payment provider. The application machines also pull 2 TB (2,048 GB) a month of images from a container registry. On money alone, through what should those images come?
hint: Price both paths for 2,048 GB.

choices.text: The NAT gateways, since they are paid for already
choices.why: Their hours are paid; their gigabytes are not: 2,048 × 0.093 = 190.46 a month.

choices.text: An interface endpoint: about 66.47 a month, against 190.46 through NAT
choices.why: Right. 45.99 for three zones plus 2,048 × 0.01 = 20.48. Far above the 554 GB break-even.

choices.text: A gateway endpoint, which is free
choices.why: A container registry is not one of the two services with a gateway endpoint.

choices.text: It makes no difference: AWS bills endpoints and NAT the same per gigabyte
choices.why: 0.01 against 0.093 is the whole difference this question rests on.

prompt: The data subnets get a route table of their own with `local` and the S3 prefix list, and no `0.0.0.0/0`. What does that give the shop besides the saving?
hint: Which way out is left?

choices.text: Faster backups, since the endpoint is in the same zone
choices.why: The lesson measured prices, not speed, and a gateway endpoint has no zone.

choices.text: The database has no path to the internet
choices.why: Right. Its only way out is the free route to S3, so a compromised database cannot call anywhere else.

choices.text: Customers can reach the database directly over S3
choices.why: A route out gives nobody a way in, and S3 does not forward connections to a VPC.

choices.text: The security groups can be removed from the database
choices.why: Routes and filters do different jobs; `db-sg` still decides who may connect.

prompt: What has to stand in front of a service the shop publishes as an endpoint service?
hint: A particular kind of load balancer.

choices.text: An Application Load Balancer
choices.why: An endpoint service takes a Network Load Balancer, or a Gateway Load Balancer for appliances.

choices.text: A Network Load Balancer
choices.why: Right. The shop's is `stock-api`, internal, in the three app subnets.

choices.text: An internet gateway
choices.why: PrivateLink keeps the traffic off the internet; no gateway to it is involved.

choices.text: A NAT gateway in each zone
choices.why: NAT is for connections out to the internet. Consumers reach the service through their own endpoint.

prompt: Suppose staging's VPC had been given `10.20.0.0/16` too, the same range as production. Could it still use the stock API through PrivateLink?
hint: What does PrivateLink join, and what does it not?

choices.text: After staging adds a secondary range that does not overlap
choices.why: No range has to change. Overlap matters for peering and Transit Gateway, which route between ranges.

choices.text: No: overlapping ranges cannot be joined in any way
choices.why: They cannot be routed to each other; PrivateLink does not route between them.

choices.text: Yes: nothing routes between the two ranges
choices.why: Right. Staging sees an interface in its own subnet; production sees connections from its load balancer's addresses.

choices.text: Yes, through a NAT gateway on each side
choices.why: NAT gateways play no part; the endpoint and the load balancer are the whole path.

prompt: What does `--acceptance-required` on the endpoint service change?
hint: Allowing a principal is one control; this is the other.

choices.text: Each consumer's endpoint waits until the provider accepts it
choices.why: Right. The shop decides each connection, not only each account.

choices.text: Consumers must accept the provider's terms before creating an endpoint
choices.why: There are no terms to accept; the acceptance is the provider's, connection by connection.

choices.text: The NLB refuses connections until a certificate is installed
choices.why: Certificates are lesson 22's subject and unrelated to the acceptance.

choices.text: It lets any AWS account connect, subject to approval
choices.why: Who may ask at all is the allowed-principals list, which names only `shop-staging`.

prompt: moto created staging's endpoint as `available` at once. What state would AWS have given it?
hint: The service requires acceptance.

choices.text: `available`, as moto did
choices.why: Not while the service requires acceptance and nobody has accepted.

choices.text: `rejected`, since staging is another account
choices.why: Staging is the allowed principal; nothing has rejected it.

choices.text: `pendingAcceptance`
choices.why: Right. It carries no traffic until the shop runs `accept-vpc-endpoint-connections`, which moto answers with an error.

choices.text: `failed`, since the two VPCs are in different accounts
choices.why: Different accounts are the case PrivateLink is built for.

prompt: Put the steps of offering the stock API to staging in order.
hint: The provider builds and opens the door; the consumer knocks; the provider lets it in.
items: create the internal Network Load Balancer `stock-api`
create the endpoint service on it, with acceptance required
allow the `shop-staging` account as a principal
in staging, create an interface endpoint to the service name
in production, accept the endpoint connection
trap: Acceptance comes last: there is nothing to accept until the consumer's endpoint exists.

prompt: Match each need to what serves it.
hint: The last table of the lesson.

pairs.left: reaching Systems Manager without the internet
offering one API to another account, one way
machines of two VPCs talking freely

prompt: A new account's VPC runs batch jobs that read and write S3 and call nothing else. Which arrangement gives the jobs what they need for the least money?
hint: Which way to S3 is free, and what else would cost by the hour?

choices.text: A NAT gateway per zone, as in production
choices.why: That is 214.62 a month before the 0.093 per gigabyte, for traffic a free route can carry.

choices.text: An interface endpoint for S3 in each zone
choices.why: It works, at 45.99 a month plus 0.01 a gigabyte; the gateway kind does the same for nothing.

choices.text: One shared NAT gateway, since the jobs can survive a zone
choices.why: Cheaper than three, and still 71.54 a month plus 0.093 a gigabyte for nothing the jobs need.

choices.text: A gateway endpoint for S3 in their route tables, and no route to the internet
choices.why: Right. Free by the hour and the gigabyte, and the jobs end up with no path to the internet at all.

prompt: Which of these cost nothing in the price lists the lessons read? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of the five are charged by the hour.

choices.text: A gateway endpoint
choices.why: Right. No hourly line and no line per gigabyte.

choices.text: An interface endpoint's hours
choices.why: 0.021 an hour for each zone it sits in.

choices.text: The gigabytes S3 receives through a gateway endpoint
choices.why: Right. That is the saving of the backups, 95.23 a month.

choices.text: An internet gateway's hours
choices.why: Right. Lesson 17: it has no hourly charge; its bytes are data transfer.

choices.text: A NAT gateway's hours
choices.why: 0.093 an hour, which is why sharing one was tempting.
